background: For chores, the envious agent hypothetically removes a task from its own bundle; for goods, removal is from the envied bundle. Negating utilities therefore does not simply transfer the known goods proofs. With additive costs, higher-agent counterexamples now rule out a universal existence theorem, while three-agent existence remains an important separate target. Recent bounded-size existence results, approximate fairness results, and incompatibility with Pareto efficiency each answer different questions. This entry fixes three agents, additive nonnegative costs, complete allocation, and exact EFX, so that progress can be compared within one model.
short_statement: For three agents dividing indivisible chores with additive costs, complete EFX is known for at most eight chores. The arbitrary-size existence question remains.
full_statement:
Let $N=\{1,2,3\}$ and let $M$ be a finite set of indivisible chores. Agent $i$ has nonnegative additive costs $c_i(S)=\sum_{g\in S}c_i(g)$. A complete allocation partitions $M$ into $(X_1,X_2,X_3)$, allowing empty bundles.

Use the standard all-chores EFX convention: for every $i,j$ and every $g\in X_i$, including $c_i(g)=0$, $$c_i(X_i\setminus\{g\})\le c_i(X_j).$$ Removing a chore is hypothetical, and from the envious agent's own bundle. This is stronger than checking only positive-cost deletions.

Does such an allocation always exist for three agents and an arbitrary number of chores? Counterexamples for four or more agents do not settle this question.
known_results:
Wentao He and Biaoshuai Tao (arXiv:2606.08872v2, July 2026), Theorems 1-3, give additive counterexamples for every $n\ge4$, using three positive cost values. They also prove four-agent bi-valued EFX existence and bi-valued EFX/Pareto-optimality incompatibility for $n\ge4$. This is not a bi-valued existence theorem for all $n$.

Xinkai Zhang, 'EFX Allocations for Three Agents and Seven or Eight Chores' (arXiv:2609.10585v2, October 2026), Theorems 1.1-1.2, handles seven and eight chores with arbitrary nonnegative additive costs. Together with the earlier $m\le2n$ theorem, this covers three-agent instances with at most eight chores. The computer-assisted certificates were not replayed here.

Jugal Garg and Aniket Murhekar (arXiv:2507.19461v1) prove existence of multiplicative 2-EFX for any number of additive agents: after deleting any one owned chore, its remaining cost is at most twice the comparison bundle's cost. This does not mean deleting two chores.

Remaining open problem. Prove complete exact EFX for three additive agents without bounding the number of chores, or give a counterexample.

where_posed.text: Nonexistence for chores under superadditive costs (n=3) established in Christoforidis, Santorinaios, 'On the Pursuit of EFX for Chores: Non-Existence and Approximations', IJCAI 2024; the sharper additive-costs, general-n nonexistence result (n>=4) is due to He, Tao, 'EFX for Additive Chores: Nonexistence, Pareto Incompatibility, and Bi-Valued Existence', arXiv, June 2026, which explicitly frames itself as resolving 'the long-standing open problem for the existence of EFX allocations with additive cost functions'; the n=3 additive case is left open by both.
where_posed.quote: We consider the fair division problem of indivisible chores and resolve the long-standing open problem for the existence of EFX allocations with additive cost functions. We show that, even for tri-valued additive cost functions, for every n≥4, there exists an instance with n agents where no EFX allocation exists. Our counterexample only uses three types of chores, which is also tight on the number of types, as an EFX allocation is known to exist for two types of chores.

progress.summary: The checked arXiv theorem covers up to eight chores. Neither higher-agent counterexamples nor multiplicative approximation resolves unrestricted three-agent existence.

counterexample_rationale: The problem is specifically about a small, finite case ($n=3$ agents, additive costs); the 2026 nonexistence breakthrough for $n\ge4$ was itself found via an explicit small hand/computer-aided construction (three cost values, few chores), and the same search methodology (careful case analysis or automated SAT/ILP search over small instances) is a natural and directly applicable route to settling $n=3$ either way.
alphaevolve_rationale: Because the remaining question is about one exact, small finite case ($n=3$), an evolutionary/LLM-guided search over cost matrices combined with a fast EFX-feasibility oracle (brute-force or SAT-based, since $n=3$ keeps the allocation space and the number of EFX inequalities small) is very well matched to this problem: it could either surface an $n=3$ counterexample (mirroring how He-Tao's $n\ge4$ counterexample was found) or, by exhaustively failing to find one across systematically varied instances, build strong empirical evidence for an existence conjecture that a human could then try to prove.

literature.synthesis: The direction of deletion matters: goods EFX removes from the envied bundle, whereas chores EFX removes from one's own bundle. Existence, approximate fairness, and compatibility with Pareto efficiency are separate questions. The unrestricted three-agent target survives both the higher-agent negative result and the recent bounded-size positive results.

reviewed.result: First EFX nonexistence example for chores: 6 items, 3 agents, superadditive costs; also shows unbounded approximation ratio and NP-completeness of EFX existence checking for monotone costs; establishes positive results for monotone costs when items $\le n+2$.

agent_guidance.suitable_approaches: Because the target case is fixed and small ($n=3$, unrestricted additive costs), the most promising approaches are: (1) adapt the He-Tao tri-valued construction technique — try to push their nonexistence gadget down to $n=3$, or prove structurally why it cannot go below $n=4$ (which would itself be informative); (2) exhaustive or SAT/ILP-based search over small 3-agent additive-cost instances (bounded number of chores, small integer costs) to find a counterexample directly, mirroring the SAT-solving methodology used for the analogous goods problem; (3) attempt to extend the existing $n=3$ positive results (bi-valued, personalized bi-valued, identical-ordering) toward general additive costs by relaxing their structural assumptions one at a time to see where the proof breaks.
agent_guidance.verification_notes: Verify completeness, additivity, nonnegative costs, and every owned-chore deletion, including zero-cost chores. A nonexistence proof must rule out all allocations, not only balanced bundle sizes. Do not confuse multiplicative 2-EFX with EF2X. Computational existence certificates require a correct encoding, exhaustive case coverage, and independently checkable unsatisfiability proofs. The higher-agent counterexamples do not settle the three-agent target.
